title: SPIKE-RL: Video-LLMs meet Bayesian Surprise
one_liner: A video-watching system learns to spot surprising moments by tracking what it expects versus what it sees, then watches those moments more carefully.
lead: Most video AI models watch every frame the same way, like a person scrolling past a boring video. SPIKE learns to notice surprising moments—when reality clashes with what it expected to see. SPIKE-RL pushes this further by using reward signals from video captions to refine what counts as surprising, then allocates more viewing time to those critical frames.

paras: Video understanding systems sample frames uniformly—they look at every fifth frame or every tenth frame, treating all moments equally. But real videos pack their meaning unevenly: two minutes of someone walking, then five seconds where they trip and fall. The tripping moment carries the narrative.

A naive approach: sample more frames everywhere. But that wastes compute on routine scenes. A beginner might try hand-crafted rules (detect motion, flag rare objects) but those rules break on new video types. What works for sports fails on cooking; what works for accidents fails on plot twists in dialogue.

callout.html: Models need a principled way to spot which frames matter without hand-tuned rules, using only what the model itself observes.

steps.text: The model forms an expectation of what the next frame will show.
Observe the real frame. Compute how far it deviates from the expectation.
The surprise score is how much seeing this frame updates the model's beliefs.
If the caption flags surprise (like oops or wow), reinforce that the surprise detector is correct.
Sample more frames from high-surprise windows, fewer from routine windows.

paras: SPIKE changes the frame sampling strategy from uniform (take every Nth frame) to surprise-weighted (take more frames when the video contradicts expectations).

hidden.h2: Bayesian surprise: how much reality rewrites your beliefs
hidden.name: Bayesian surprise (belief update magnitude)
paras: Bayesian surprise is not a feeling. It is a measurable quantity: how much observing a new piece of evidence should shift your beliefs. If you predict the next frame shows a person walking and the frame shows a person walking, surprise is zero. If you predict walking and the frame shows falling, surprise is large.

SPIKE estimates this by feeding the model a frame and asking: how much did your prediction change? A large change means high surprise. SPIKE-RL refines this by labelling surprising moments (using video captions like oops or wow) and training the model to score those moments higher, using GRPO (a reward-based nudging method to align the model's surprise detector with human-labeled ground truth).

heat.caption: Darker means higher surprise. Highlighted frames show moments captions marked as surprising.

reads.html: Bayesian surprise is how much reality contradicts what you expected. A bigger contradiction means a bigger surprise score.
SPIKE measures Bayesian surprise as the belief update (change in model predictions) triggered by new visual evidence. SPIKE-RL refines the surprise scorer using GRPO and caption-based rewards.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: connecting belief and reality
paras: Here is the core loop. A video-understanding model builds a running picture of what is happening. When a new frame arrives, the model first predicts what the next frame should show based on the current picture. Then it observes the actual frame. If the actual frame matches the prediction, the model's beliefs are stable (low surprise). If the actual frame conflicts with the prediction, the model must shift its beliefs by a large amount (high surprise).

Surprise is valuable because it flags narrative-critical moments. Routine scenes (person walking, person talking) produce low surprise and can be sampled sparsely. Turning points (person stumbles, person receives news) produce high surprise and need more frames. By allocating more samples to high-surprise windows, the model sees the full context around critical events without wasting compute on repetition.

SPIKE-RL adds a refinement: caption rewards. If a video is captioned with words like oops or wow, those labels signal which moments humans found surprising. The model trains to align its surprise detector with those labels using GRPO—a method that nudges the model's predictions to maximize a reward signal. This tunes the surprise detector without requiring manual annotation of every frame.

stages.s: Model predicts next frame from context
Observe real frame and measure prediction error
SPIKE-RL: Align surprise with caption labels via rewards
Frame sampling weights (more for high surprise)

math.words: Surprise equals the size of the prediction error scaled by how uncertain the model was. High error plus high uncertainty equals high surprise.
math.equation: surprise_t = log p(frame_t | context) - log p_old_t
symbols: surprise score at time t (how much beliefs shift)
log probability model assigns to the observed frame given what it has seen
log probability the model predicted before seeing the frame
all the video frames seen up to time t

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Frame 1: Model predicts next frame with 95% confidence. Actual frame matches. Prediction log prob = -0.05. Old guess log prob = -0.05. Surprise = -0.05 - (-0.05) = 0 (no surprise).

Frame 10 (trip moment): Model predicts walking with 90% confidence. Actual frame shows falling. Prediction log prob = -2.3. Old guess log prob = -0.1. Surprise = -2.3 - (-0.1) = -2.2 (magnitude 2.2: high surprise).
The math compares the log probabilities: a large gap means the observed frame was far less likely than predicted, so surprise is high.

math.note: The surprise score measures how much the real frame contradicts the model's expectation, which is exactly what the method uses to identify which frames deserve more viewing time.

items.html: If SPIKE-RL trains only on videos with captions, it may learn spurious patterns in the captions (e.g. oops always means falling) rather than genuine visual surprise. On new video types without those captions, performance drops.

items.b: Routine scenes with unseen content fool it.
items.html: A brand-new background or object (rare but not narrative-critical) can trigger high surprise. The model then wastes extra frames on it. The surprise detector cannot distinguish between plot-turning new things and incidental unseen things.

Not every surprising moment is labeled. SPIKE-RL trains on the labels it sees, so unlabeled surprises remain underweighted. If some video types are over-labeled (e.g. action videos get more oops tags), the model learns a skewed surprise model.

items.b: Done right: combine visual surprise with semantic cues.
items.html: Pair the Bayesian surprise signal (pure visual prediction error) with semantic signals from captions, using domain labels to prevent overfitting. Validate on out-of-domain videos to catch surprise mislabelling.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a mini video sequence where a model predicts the next frame. Insert a turning point (e.g. a person suddenly changes pose or background shifts). Measure the prediction error at every frame. Then run the model on:1) uniform frame sampling and 2) surprise-weighted sampling (allocate 5x frames to the top-10% surprise scores). Measure how many frames are needed to answer a downstream task (e.g. what happened to this object) at a fixed accuracy.
demo.closing: The demo must show that surprise-weighted sampling needs fewer total frames to answer the same question correctly, because it concentrates viewing effort on the moments that matter.
